posts.title: The November changeover
posts.excerpt: November is when heating takes over from cooling, and the changeover is the one visit we never move.
posts.content:
November is when heating takes over from cooling, and the changeover is the one visit we never move. Controls are tuned, dampers are set for winter and the filters are changed before the first cold week.

Between visits, a facilities manager can check that the plant room is clear, the rooftop access hatch closes properly and nothing is stored against the units. Write what you see in the log; Tomás will read it first.

posts.title: Halvorsen House
posts.excerpt: How a structured maintenance contract keeps nine rooftop units operating smoothly across six commercial office floors in Rotterdam.
posts.content:
Halvorsen House is a commercial office property of six floors situated in Rotterdam, accommodating multiple professional tenants whose daily operations depend entirely on reliable indoor climate control. The building's mechanical installation comprises nine rooftop condenser units paired with ducted air-handling equipment and ceiling distribution cassettes. Like many multi-tenant commercial properties, the occupants inside give little thought to the plant room or the rooftop machinery until a fan bearing squeals or indoor temperatures climb unexpectedly during a business presentation. When Kuki Climate B.V. took over the maintenance contract for Halvorsen House in 2019, our objective was to eliminate those unpredictable disruptions through disciplined preventative routines.

The facility operates on our quarterly maintenance contract, supplemented by monthly attendances during June, July, and August when cooling demands peak. The contract began with a comprehensive sixty-minute survey hour conducted by our contract manager Leila Haddad and lead service technician Tomás Ribeiro. They walked the six occupied floors, accessed the roof, catalogued all nine nameplates, and graded the physical condition of each unit from A to D. The resulting written report revealed several clogged condensate drain trays and uneven refrigeration pressures on three aging condenser circuits. By identifying these vulnerabilities before summer trading began, we established a baseline maintenance log that has guided every subsequent site visit since 2019.

A typical maintenance visit at Halvorsen House begins early in the morning, following our 07:00 depot briefing at Koelhuisweg. Our service van arrives on site by 07:40 so technicians can inspect rooftop condensers before direct sun creates harsh working conditions and thermal distortion. Tomás Ribeiro inspects the fan assemblies, checks belt tension, clears airborne debris from coil fins with low-pressure wash equipment, and inspects electrical contactors for pitting. Meanwhile, Samuel Mensah, our F-gas certified refrigeration technician, connects digital manifold gauges to verify suction pressures, superheat levels, and subcooling values across the nine separate refrigerant circuits, ensuring no slow leaks compromise seasonal performance or environmental compliance.

Once mechanical work on the roof concludes and internal building loads stabilise, technicians move indoors after 11:00 to inspect air distribution grilles and plant room controls. Daichi Mori configured the building's controls schedule to balance fresh-air ventilation with energy conservation, preventing simultaneous heating and cooling conflicts across different tenanted suites. Technicians inspect filter differential pressure gauges, replace pleated filters as scheduled, and verify that condensate pumps drain freely into internal soil stacks. Each task is completed methodically, avoiding noise or disruption in corridors and tenanted office suites.

Before departing for our 16:30 handover at the service desk, the technicians complete the site service log. At Halvorsen House, this record consists of one durable physical binder stored on the shelf beside the main chiller panel, alongside a shared digital PDF record transmitted directly to the building's facilities manager. The log documents exact operating pressures, filter replacement dates, motor running currents, and technician signatures. For the facilities team at Halvorsen House, this operational continuity means no guesswork, no forgotten maintenance history, and plant that remains dependable through every season.

posts.title: Noordpoort Health Centre
posts.excerpt: Noordpoort Health Centre is a two-floor clinic with two air handling units and six ceiling cassettes.
posts.content:
Noordpoort Health Centre is a two-floor clinic with two air handling units and six ceiling cassettes. The contract has been monthly since 2021, because the consulting rooms need quiet, clean air every working day.

At each visit we read the filter pressure drop and log it next to last month's figure, check the controls against the schedule the practice manager gave us, and flush the cassette drains on a rota. Samuel Mensah does the refrigerant check once a year.

Readings that stay comparable from month to month are what let us change a filter before anyone in a consulting room notices.

posts.title: Maasweg Primary School
posts.excerpt: Maasweg Primary School has three rooftop units and a cassette unit in most classrooms.
posts.content:
Maasweg Primary School has three rooftop units and a cassette unit in most classrooms. The contract has been quarterly since 2022, and the two visits that matter most, the March cooling start-up and the November heating changeover, are booked into school holidays.

The caretaker keeps the binder in the plant room cupboard and signs each visit before the technician leaves. Jonas Becker, our second-year apprentice, has done the filter change there twice under supervision.

No lesson has been interrupted by a visit yet, and that is the way we would like to keep it.

posts.title: What goes in the log
posts.excerpt: The log is one binder in the plant room and one shared PDF: pressures, dates, parts and a signature.
posts.content:
The log is one binder in the plant room and one shared PDF. Every visit adds a page: the date, the units checked, operating pressures, filters changed, parts fitted and the technician’s signature.

The point is not the paperwork. It is that the next person, whether ours or yours, can see what was done and what was noticed without asking anyone.

posts.title: Drains before summer
posts.excerpt: A blocked condensate tray is the commonest cause of a ceiling stain in the first hot week.
posts.content:
A blocked condensate tray is the commonest cause of a ceiling stain in the first hot week. In May we lift the tile, clear the tray and check the fall of the drain line.

If you have ceiling cassettes, look for water marks around them and tell the service desk before the heat arrives. It is a ten-minute job in May and a long afternoon in July.
